builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents
summary: SatisFix replaces generic self-correction or reflection loops with a two-step prompt procedure in which the coding agent first reports implementation choices where it knowingly deviated from a requirement and the reason, then verifies each choice against the task description. It costs additional inference passes per task (more tokens and latency through the same API or local model, no extra infrastructure) plus prompt-engineering integration into an existing agent framework. It can fail when the agent does not actually report its satisficing choices, when the checking step is biased toward the same rationalizations the paper identifies, and gains may not transfer to task types or backbones beyond those evaluated.
rationale: The method is a prompt-level addition compatible with third-party APIs and existing agent frameworks, but its gains are benchmark-specific and depend on the backbone model's willingness to surface its own deviations, so it warrants a workload-specific pilot before production adoption.
technique: Self-reported requirement checking for coding agents

claims.statement: SatisFix replaces generic self-correction or reflection loops with a two-step prompt procedure in which the coding agent first reports implementation choices where it knowingly deviated from a requirement and the reason, then verifies each choice against the task description. It costs additional inference passes per task (more tokens and latency through the same API or local model, no extra infrastructure) plus prompt-engineering integration into an existing agent framework. It can fail when the agent does not actually report its satisficing choices, when the checking step is biased toward the same rationalizations the paper identifies, and gains may not transfer to task types or backbones beyond those evaluated.

Improves pass@1 by an average of 5.09% on DeepSWE and 7.06% on the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro over the base agent, and outperforms the best self-correction baseline by 3.98% on DeepSWE; both components contribute per ablation.
